guide.title: Trevi, Rome: the Fountain, the Acqua Vergine and the Quirinal
guide.intro: Trevi is R. II, the second of Rome's rioni. Roma Capitale records the Fontana di Trevi under Rione: Trevi, and records the fountain as the terminal mostra of the Acqua Vergine, the aqueduct inaugurated by Agrippa in 19 BC that feeds the monumental fountains of the Baroque city. Roma Capitale now charges for access to the fountain's inner perimeter and caps the number of people inside it; the arrangements are set out below. From the fountain the rione climbs to the Quirinal, where the palace that housed popes, then kings, and now the President of the Italian Republic stands on a square Trevi shares with Monti. In between are a palace remodelled by Borromini, a covered passage of the 1880s, and a church that keeps the precordia of twenty-two popes.

sections.heading: Water: the aqueduct, the fountain and the city underneath
sections.body:
Trevi's subject is water, and the water arrives by a Roman aqueduct. Roma Capitale records the Acquedotto Vergine under Rione: II - Trevi: inaugurated in 19 BC by Agrippa, drawing from the Agro Lucullano near the eighth mile of the via Collatina, at the modern locality of Salone, and running over 20 kilometres, predominantly underground, to end in the Campo Marzio. It feeds the monumental fountains of the Baroque city, among them the Fontana di Trevi, which in the modern age is its terminal mostra. Part of it is visible above ground in the rione: at via del Nazareno three partly buried travertine arches in rusticated blocks survive at the sides of a larger fornix, identified with the arch Claudius had raised to mark his victory over the Germans, above which is set the inscription recording his rebuilding of the aqueduct in AD 46. Roma Capitale describes those arches as part of the Acquedotto Vergine and states its rione as II - Trevi; no source we fetched places them in another rione.

The fountain itself is eighteenth-century civic architecture built against the façade of Palazzo Poli. Roma Capitale gives the authors as Nicola Salvi and Giuseppe Pannini and the dates as 1732-1762, in travertine, marble, plaster, stucco and metals, and records that Pannini concluded the construction, partly modifying the scogliera and regularising the central basins. It also records an earlier attempt: in 1640, for Urban VIII and in step with the enlargement of the square, Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed a fountain on the present orientation, of which only an exedra base and a basin were built, set against buildings later absorbed into Palazzo Poli.

Under the buildings on the far side of the same square, excavation at the end of the 1990s, during restructuring and consolidation work, uncovered traces of an insula of Neronian date fronting the Vicus Caprarius, converted partly into a patrician domus in the middle of the fourth century and partly into a large cistern collecting the Acqua Vergine. Remains of twelfth- and thirteenth-century buildings were found above and partly overlying them, and traces of that urbanisation survive in the medieval portico on the side of the square facing the fountain. The area has been reorganised and is open to visitors as La Città dell'Acqua.

sections.heading: The Quirinal, and the treaty buildings on Italian soil
sections.body:
The Palazzo del Quirinale was a papal residence from 1605 to 1870, a royal residence from 1871 to 1946, and has been the residence of the President of the Italian Republic since; the Italian Wikipedia article ties the two changes to the presa di Roma of 20 September 1870 and to the referendum of 2 June 1946. Its construction is not settled. One Italian Wikipedia article gives 1573-1583 with Ottaviano Mascherino as first architect; another says it was built in the years 1573-1585 by Martino Longhi il Vecchio and then, from 1578, by Ottaviano Mascherino. Sources differ, and this guide does not choose between them.

The square in front of it belongs to two rioni. The Italian Wikipedia article, citing Sergio Delli, Le strade di Roma, 3rd ed., Newton Compton, 1988, p. 809, places Piazza del Quirinale between Via del Quirinale and Via XXIV Maggio, nei rioni I Monti e II Trevi. From the Middle Ages and still into the nineteenth century it was known as Piazza di Monte Cavallo. The fountain and the obelisk standing in it are in Trevi: Roma Capitale states Rione: Trevi for the Fontana di Monte Cavallo, and records that in 1786 Pius VI had the Egyptian granite obelisk taken from the Mausoleum of Augustus in the Campo Marzio set between the Dioscuri, to a design by the architect Giovanni Antinori.

Buildings in Trevi appear in the Lateran Treaty of 1929 in three different ways, and the differences matter. Article 15 names the palazzi della Dataria among the buildings which, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoy the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign States: that is a diplomatic-headquarters immunity granted on Italian soil, not a piece of Vatican City and not a border. Article 14's third alinea instead transfers to the Holy See the ex-conventual buildings in Rome annexed to the Basilica dei Santi XII Apostoli, and Article 15 reaches only the properties indicated in Article 13 and in the first and second alinea of Article 14, so those buildings fall outside Article 15 altogether. Article 16 then provides that the properties named in the three preceding articles, together with the buildings used as the seats of a named list of pontifical institutes including the Università Gregoriana and the Istituto Biblico, shall never be subjected to encumbrances or to expropriation for reasons of public utility save by prior agreement with the Holy See, and shall be exempt from taxation, ordinary and extraordinary, whether to the State or to any other body. That is a property and tax provision. It is not extraterritoriality and it is not diplomatic immunity. The Gregoriana and the Biblicum both stand in rione Trevi, on Italian soil; neither is in Vatican City and neither is extraterritorial.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Trevi is bounded by streets rather than by anything you can see, and the Italian Wikipedia articles for the neighbouring rioni name them. Colonna's article gives its boundary with Trevi as piazza Barberini, via del Tritone, largo Chigi, piazza Colonna and via del Corso. Trevi's own article gives its boundary with Monti as via del Quirinale, piazza del Quirinale, via Ventiquattro Maggio and largo Magnanapoli. Via del Corso is crossed by four rioni and belongs to none of them; San Marcello al Corso and Palazzo Mancini are in Trevi while the Galleria Alberto Sordi, on the same street, is in Colonna.

Two of the rione's set pieces stand on ground shared with a neighbour. Piazza Barberini lies across Trevi, Colonna and Ludovisi, and Colonna's article names it as its boundary with Trevi. Piazza del Quirinale is shared with Monti. The buildings and fountains described here stand in Trevi even where their square does not.

At the fountain, Roma Capitale routes visitors in by the central staircase and out through the gate on the via dei Crociferi side, and caps the inner perimeter at about 400 people at a time; the charge, the free list and the hours are in the entry for the fountain below. For the aqueduct, entry is only to accompanied groups, by booking on 060608, and Roma Capitale states that the site is temporarily closed for works, so check before making the trip. We could not reach the Palazzo del Quirinale's own website from this network, and nothing here therefore describes whether or how the palace can be visited. The Accademia Nazionale di San Luca, the Gallerie Nazionali d'Arte Antica at Palazzo Barberini, the Galleria Colonna, the Scuderie del Quirinale, Palazzo Valentini and Vicus Caprarius each publish their own opening information on their own sites, and this guide sends you to those rather than repeating hours it could not verify.

faq.question: Do you now have to pay to see the Trevi Fountain?
faq.answer: To stand in the inner perimeter, yes, if you are a tourist or not resident in Rome or in the Città Metropolitana: Roma Capitale charges €2.00, from 09:00 to 22:00, and the charge remains in force on the first Sunday of the month. Entry is by the central staircase and exit through the gate on the via dei Crociferi side, with a maximum of about 400 people inside at a time. After the daily closure, fixed at 22:00, the fountain remains visible free of charge to everyone. Roma Capitale gives free access to residents of Rome and the Città Metropolitana on production of an identity card at the access control, to holders of the Roma MIC Card, to people with disabilities and one companion, to tour guides on production of a valid badge, and to children up to 5. Checked 2 September 2026.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Acqua Vergine aqueduct?
faq.answer: Not at present. Roma Capitale states that the site is temporarily closed for works. Its published arrangements are entry only to accompanied groups, a maximum of 20 people per visit, with booking obligatory on 060608 between 09:00 and 19:00; individual visits are also possible, always by booking on 060608, on a calendar published by Roma Capitale. Tariffs are €4.00 full and €3.00 reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of a valid document attesting residence, and for MIC card holders. A guided tour is not included in the entrance price. Checked 2 September 2026.

faq.question: Is the Palazzo della Dataria part of Vatican City?
faq.answer: No. Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929 names the Palazzo della Dataria among the buildings which, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoy the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign states. The palace stands in via della Dataria, in rione Trevi. It is on Italian soil: it is not in Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, it is not a border, and visitors in it are subject to Italian law. What its status is today is not established by any source we could reach.

faq.question: Are Piazza del Quirinale and Piazza Barberini in Trevi?
faq.answer: Both are shared. The Italian Wikipedia article on Piazza del Quirinale, citing Sergio Delli's Le strade di Roma, places the square nei rioni I Monti e II Trevi. Piazza Barberini lies across three rioni, Trevi, Colonna and Ludovisi, and the Italian Wikipedia article on rione Colonna names the piazza as Colonna's boundary with Trevi. The monuments standing in them are a separate question: Roma Capitale states Rione: Trevi for the Fontana di Monte Cavallo, and the Fontana del Tritone in Piazza Barberini stands on the Trevi side.

faq.question: Which church keeps the popes' precordia?
faq.answer: Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi, on Piazza di Trevi. The Italian Wikipedia article records that it preserves the precordia removed during the embalming of popes, the urns of 22 popes from Sixtus V to Leo XIII, and that they are not displayed to the faithful. The same article quotes Belli's phrase for the collection, un museo de corate e de ciorcelli. It is precordia, not hearts, and there is nothing to see.

faq.question: Is the Palazzo Colonna in the rione called Colonna?
faq.answer: No. The palace on Via della Pilotta and the Galleria Colonna inside it stand in rione Trevi, and the research done for rione Colonna positively confirms that neither is in that rione. A second name trap works the same way: Palazzo Chigi-Odescalchi, on Piazza dei Santi Apostoli, is in Trevi and is not the Palazzo Chigi on Piazza Colonna.

photos.title: Fontana di Trevi
photos.description: The Fontana di Trevi seen from the square, built against the facade of Palazzo Poli as the terminal mostra of the Acqua Vergine aqueduct.
photos.author: Diego Delso

places.name: Fontana di Trevi
places.summary: A monumental fountain set against the façade of Palazzo Poli and serving as the terminal mostra of the Acqua Vergine aqueduct. Roma Capitale states Rione: Trevi for it, gives the authors as Nicola Salvi and Giuseppe Pannini and the dates as 1732-1762, and lists the materials as travertine, marble, plaster, stucco and metals.
places.history:
Roma Capitale records that in 1640, for Urban VIII and in step with the enlargement of the square, Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed a fountain on the present orientation, of which only an exedra base and a basin were built, set against buildings later absorbed into Palazzo Poli.

Roma Capitale dates to 1732 the competition Clement XII called for the fountain; the Italian Wikipedia article dates the competition to 1731. Work began in 1732. Roma Capitale records that the pope chose, among the entries, Nicola Salvi's most monumental design, the one of least prejudice to the palace behind. The Italian Wikipedia article records that the commission passed in 1759 to Pietro Bracci, assisted by his son Virginio, and that the fountain was inaugurated in 1762. Roma Capitale records that Giuseppe Pannini concluded the construction, partly modifying the scogliera and regularising the central basins.

Roma Capitale's restoration chronology: a restoration in 1989-1991; maintenance of the central section in 1999; a restoration funded by FENDI begun in 2014 and completed after seventeen months in 2015, inaugurated 3 November; and a maintenance intervention from October to December 2024 under the PNRR - Caput Mundi programme, recorded as Manutenzione straordinaria di alcune fontane monumentali del Centro Storico di Roma, n. 323.

Visiting. Roma Capitale charges €2.00 for access to the inner perimeter of the fountain, for tourists and for people not resident in Rome or in the Città Metropolitana. The charge applies from 09:00 to 22:00 and remains in force on the first Sunday of the month. Access to the inner perimeter is guaranteed to a maximum of about 400 people at a time, with entry by the central staircase and exit through the gate on the via dei Crociferi side. After the daily closure, fixed at 22:00, the fountain remains visible free of charge to everyone. Roma Capitale gives free access to residents of Rome and the Città Metropolitana on production of an identity card at the access control, to holders of the Roma MIC Card, to people with disabilities and one companion, to tour guides on production of a valid badge, and to children up to 5. Tickets are sold online, at the Musei Civici, Tourist Info Points and affiliated outlets, and at the fountain entrance by card only. Roma Capitale publishes hours at fontanaditrevi.roma.it. Checked 2 September 2026.

places.name: Acquedotto Vergine (Aqua Virgo)
places.summary: The Roman aqueduct that supplies the fountains of this part of the city, recorded by Roma Capitale under Rione: II - Trevi. It feeds the monumental fountains of the Baroque city, among them the Fontana di Trevi, which in the modern age is its terminal mostra. Arches of it survive at via del Nazareno.
places.history:
Roma Capitale records the aqueduct as inaugurated in 19 BC by Agrippa, with its sources in the Agro Lucullano near the eighth mile of the via Collatina, at the modern locality of Salone, and a course of over 20 kilometres, predominantly underground, ending in the Campo Marzio.

At via del Nazareno three partly buried travertine arches in rusticated blocks survive at the sides of a larger fornix, identified with the arch Claudius had raised to mark his victory over the Germans, above which is set the inscription recording his rebuilding of the aqueduct in AD 46. Roma Capitale records the Acquedotto Vergine under Rione: II - Trevi and describes the arches at via del Nazareno as part of it. No source we fetched places these arches in another rione.

Roma Capitale also records two further travertine fornici beneath Palazzo Sciarra. That is the Palazzo Sciarra on via del Corso, which is not the Palazzo Sciarra Colonna di Carbognano in Trevi; the two names are close and the two buildings are not the same, so that pair of arches is not a Trevi feature.

Visiting: Roma Capitale states that the site is temporarily closed for works. Its published arrangements are entry only to accompanied groups, a maximum of 20 people per visit, with booking obligatory on 060608 between 09:00 and 19:00; individual visits also possible, always by booking on 060608, on a calendar published by Roma Capitale. Tariffs: €4.00 full, €3.00 reduced; free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of a valid document attesting residence, and for MIC card holders. A guided tour is not included in the entrance price. Checked 2 September 2026.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi
places.summary: The parish church on Piazza di Trevi, in rione Trevi, standing on the same square as the fountain. Its popular name was il canneto, because its façade is decorated with 18 columns.
places.history:
Its medieval name was Sant'Anastasio de Trivio; from 1570 it has been known under the double dedication. The Italian Wikipedia article's infobox gives 1644 for the start of construction and 1650 for its completion, and the article records that the original church was rebuilt in Baroque form at the order of Cardinal Mazarin and was erected a parish at that time.

The same article says the church came to be known as the parrocchia pontificia for two reasons: because the Palazzo del Quirinale, the pope's residence, was in the area, and because the precordia of the pontiffs were kept in the church. It preserves them still, not displayed to the faithful: the precordia removed during the embalming of popes, in the urns of 22 popes, from Sixtus V to Leo XIII. Belli's phrase for them, quoted in the same article, is un museo de corate e de ciorcelli. They are precordia rather than hearts, and there is nothing on show.

places.name: Vicus Caprarius - La Città dell'Acqua
places.summary: An underground archaeological area beneath the buildings on the side of Piazza di Trevi facing the fountain, presented to visitors as La Città dell'Acqua.
places.history:
Excavation at the end of the 1990s, during restructuring and consolidation work, uncovered traces of an insula of Neronian date fronting the Vicus Caprarius, converted partly into a patrician domus in the middle of the 4th century and partly into a large cistern collecting the Acqua Vergine. Remains of 12th- and 13th-century buildings were found above and partly overlying them, and traces of that urbanisation survive in the medieval portico on the side of the square facing the fountain. The area is reorganised and open to visitors.

No hours are given here. The site publishes its own at vicuscaprarius.com, and the hours we found elsewhere came from crowd-sourced mapping data rather than from the site itself.

places.name: Palazzo del Quirinale
places.summary: The presidential palace, on Piazza del Quirinale: a papal residence, then a royal one, and now the residence of the President of the Italian Republic. The palace is in Trevi; the square in front of it is shared with Monti.
places.history:
It was the papal residence from 1605 to 1870, the royal residence from 1871 to 1946, and has been the presidential residence since. The Italian Wikipedia article ties those changes to the presa di Roma of 20 September 1870 and to the referendum of 2 June 1946.

Its construction is not settled between sources. One Italian Wikipedia article gives 1573-1583, with Ottaviano Mascherino as the first architect; another says it was built in the years 1573-1585 by Martino Longhi il Vecchio and then, from 1578, by Ottaviano Mascherino. The two cannot both be right, so neither is given as settled.

No visiting information is given. No source states hours, ticketing, opening days or booking for the palace, so none is given here.

places.name: Piazza del Quirinale
places.summary: The square in front of the presidential palace, lying between Via del Quirinale and Via XXIV Maggio. The Italian Wikipedia article, citing Sergio Delli, Le strade di Roma, 3rd ed., Newton Compton, 1988, p. 809, places it nei rioni I Monti e II Trevi: it is shared between Monti and Trevi, and neither rione holds all of it.
places.history:
From the Middle Ages and still into the 19th century the square was known as Piazza di Monte Cavallo. Roma Capitale records that the arrangement of the square was commissioned in 1586 by Sixtus V from Domenico Fontana, who restored the Dioscuri group and moved the sculptures towards the centre of the square, facing the Strada Pia.

The Fontana dei Dioscuri and the obelisk set between the statues in 1786 stand in the square and are in Trevi; Roma Capitale states Rione: Trevi for the fountain.

places.name: Fontana dei Dioscuri (Fontana di Monte Cavallo)
places.summary: The fountain at the foot of the colossal Dioscuri group on Piazza del Quirinale. Roma Capitale states Rione: Trevi for it, attributes it to Giacomo della Porta and Raffaele Stern, dates it 1589 and 1818, gives its materials as granite and marble, and records its original supply as the acquedotto Felice.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's account: the arrangement of the square was commissioned in 1586 by Sixtus V from Domenico Fontana, who restored the Dioscuri group and moved the sculptures towards the centre of the square, facing the Strada Pia; in 1589 a first fountain fed by the Acqua Felice was placed at the foot of the statues, and it was removed in 1783; the present fountain was made only in 1818, reusing a large grey granite basin that had been in the Roman Forum, with Raffaele Stern as consultant. The Italian Wikipedia article on the Fontana dei Dioscuri instead names Domenico Fontana as the author of the fountain itself.

On the origin of the sculptures the sources do not agree. The Italian Wikipedia articles say the group came from the Terme di Costantino. Roma Capitale's page does not say this; it states only that the group had stood on the Quirinal hill since antiquity.

Roma Capitale records a restoration in 2016 and an extraordinary maintenance intervention in 2025 under the PNRR - Caput Mundi programme.

places.name: Obelisco del Quirinale
places.summary: The Egyptian granite obelisk standing between the two Dioscuri on Piazza del Quirinale. The Italian Wikipedia article describes it as red Aswan granite, 14.63 m high and 28.94 m with its base, carrying no hieroglyphic inscriptions.
places.history: In 1786 Pius VI had the obelisk, taken from the Mausoleum of Augustus in the Campo Marzio, set between the Dioscuri, to a design by the architect Giovanni Antinori. Roma Capitale records this and the Italian Wikipedia article corroborates it independently.

places.name: Scuderie del Quirinale
places.summary: The former papal stables on the Quirinal, now a venue for art exhibitions.
places.history:
The Italian Wikipedia article on Piazza del Quirinale, citing the Touring Club Italiano's Guida d'Italia, describes the Scuderie del Quirinale as an eighteenth-century building by Alessandro Specchi and Ferdinando Fuga, completely restored between 1997 and 1999 and now used as a venue for art exhibitions.

Exhibitions change and no hours are given here; the venue publishes its own at scuderiequirinale.it.

places.name: Accademia Nazionale di San Luca, Palazzo Carpegna
places.address: Piazza dell'Accademia di San Luca 77, Roma RM
places.summary: An academy of artists with a gallery, in Palazzo Carpegna, which has been its seat since 1934.
places.history:
The palazzo was built between the late 16th and the first half of the 17th century for the Vaini of Imola by a pupil of Giacomo della Porta; bought around 1630 by Count Ambrogio di Carpegna, who commissioned Francesco Borromini for enlargement and remodelling; and completed under Francesco Ferrari between 1732 and 1736.

On the academy's own beginning the sources differ, and no single founding year is given here. The Italian Wikipedia article records that before the academy existed the artists belonged to the Università dei Pittori, Miniatori e Ricamatori, a craft guild whose statutes and privileges were renewed under Sixtus IV on 17 December 1478; that the passage from Universitas to Accademia delle Arti della Pittura, della Scultura e del Disegno came on the initiative of the painter Girolamo Muziano and was officially sanctioned in 1577 by Gregory XIII, though the actual transformation was gradual; and, in its opening sentence, that the academy was founded in 1593 by Federico Zuccari, who was also its first Principe. Its infobox gives 1577.

The academy publishes its own information at accademiasanluca.it.

places.name: Galleria Sciarra
places.summary: A covered pedestrian passage in rione Trevi, a private courtyard open to the public during office hours, now in office use.
places.history:
It was built between 1886 and 1888 to a design by the architect Giulio De Angelis for Prince Maffeo Sciarra.

The address needs care. The Italian Wikipedia article gives its entrances as Via Marco Minghetti and Piazza dell'Oratorio in its text and its address as Via di Santa Maria in Via 30-31 in its infobox; the street address should be confirmed from a second source before it is relied on, so none is stated here.

places.name: Cappella della Madonna dell'Archetto
places.address: Via di San Marcello 41b, Roma RM
places.summary: A very small nineteenth-century chapel in rione Trevi, whose official name is chiesa di Santa Maria Causa Nostrae Laetitiae.
places.history: It was built in the 19th century to house an image painted on maiolica stone in 1690 by the Bolognese painter Domenico Maria Muratori. The chapel is the work of the architect Virginio Vespignani and contains paintings by Costantino Brumidi. It was solemnly inaugurated and opened to the public on 31 May 1851.

places.name: Chiesa evangelica valdese in Trevi
places.summary: The Waldensian church on via Quattro Novembre, in rione Trevi. It is not the Waldensian church in Piazza Cavour, which is in rione Prati; the two are regularly confused, including in mapping data, so check which one you are heading for.
places.history: It was built in 1883-1884 to a design by the architect Benedetto Andolfi.

places.name: Palazzo della Dataria
places.summary: A palace in via della Dataria, in rione Trevi, beside the Palazzo della Panetteria and opposite the Palazzo di San Felice. It is one of the buildings the Lateran Treaty names in terms, which makes its legal position worth stating precisely.
places.history:
Article 15 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929 names the Palazzo della Dataria among the buildings which, although forming part of the territory of the Italian State, enjoy the immunities that international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign states. The palace stands in via della Dataria, in rione Trevi. It is on Italian soil: it is not in Vatican City, it is not Vatican territory, it is not a border, and visitors in it are subject to Italian law.

What its status is today is not established by any source we could reach. The Italian Wikipedia article describes the palace as an appurtenance of the Italian presidential palace, and in the same article reports that it was assigned to the Holy See under the Lateran Pacts and sold in 1973, giving ANSA as its owner. Those statements are not consistent with one another, and we found no source that settles the question.

places.name: Palazzo della Panetteria
places.summary: A palace on Via della Dataria, in rione Trevi, standing between the Palazzo della Dataria and the Palazzo del Quirinale. Its official name is Palazzo della Famiglia Pontificia.
places.history: It was built by Paolo Posi between 1764 and 1766, Clement XIII having ordered its complete rebuilding. It is reached from the Quirinale through the Torre di Urbano VIII, the Swiss Guard tower, and it now serves as an annexe of the Quirinale. Its patron is not named here: the Italian Wikipedia article attributes the commission, in both its infobox and its body, to a pope who died in 1621, which cannot be right for a building of the 1760s.

places.name: Palazzo Chigi-Odescalchi
places.address: Piazza dei Santi Apostoli, Roma RM
places.summary: A palace on Piazza dei Santi Apostoli, in Trevi. It is not the Palazzo Chigi on Piazza Colonna, which is in rione Colonna; the names are close enough to send a visitor to the wrong building.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article records that the palace was originally Colonna property, was sold to the Ludovisi in 1622 and bought back; that it was ceded in usufruct to Cardinal Flavio Chigi in 1661 and transformed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini around 1665; and that it passed to Prince Baldassare Odescalchi in 1745.

places.name: Palazzo Baracchini
places.summary: A later nineteenth-century government building on via XX Settembre, in Trevi, and the seat of the Ministero della Difesa.
places.history: The Italian Wikipedia article dates it 1876-83 and gives the architect as Giulio Podesti.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi XII Apostoli
places.address: Piazza dei Santi Apostoli, Roma RM
places.summary: The basilica on Piazza dei Santi Apostoli, in rione Trevi. The ex-conventual buildings annexed to it are named in the Lateran Treaty, in a clause that is easy to misread.
places.history:
The third alinea of Article 14 of the Lateran Treaty of 1929 transfers to the Holy See the ex-conventual buildings in Rome annexed to the Basilica dei Santi XII Apostoli and to the churches of Sant'Andrea della Valle and San Carlo ai Catinari. Article 15 reaches only the properties indicated in Article 13 and in the first and second alinea of Article 14, so the Santi XII Apostoli buildings fall outside Article 15: they do not carry the immunities international law recognises for the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign states.

Article 16 provides that the properties named in the three preceding articles, together with the buildings used as the seats of a named list of pontifical institutes, shall never be subjected to encumbrances or to expropriation for reasons of public utility save by prior agreement with the Holy See, and shall be exempt from taxation, ordinary and extraordinary, whether to the State or to any other body. That is a property and tax provision. It is not extraterritoriality and it is not diplomatic immunity. The basilica stands on Italian soil, in rione Trevi: it is not in Vatican City and it is not Vatican territory.

places.name: Palazzo Colonna and the Galleria Colonna
places.summary: The Colonna family's palace on Via della Pilotta and the picture gallery inside it. The name is the family's and not the neighbouring rione's: both palace and gallery stand in Trevi.
places.history:
The research done for rione Colonna positively confirms that neither the palace nor the gallery is in that rione, which is the kind of correction a name makes necessary.

The gallery opens on a limited schedule that it publishes itself at galleriacolonna.it. No hours are given here, because the ones we found came from crowd-sourced mapping data rather than from the institution.

places.name: Palazzo Barberini and the Gallerie Nazionali d'Arte Antica
places.address: Via delle Quattro Fontane 13, Roma RM
places.summary: The palace on Via delle Quattro Fontane, in Trevi, and the seat of the Gallerie Nazionali d'Arte Antica.
places.history:
The palace and its garden are in Trevi. The square that carries the same family name is not: Piazza Barberini lies across Trevi, Colonna and Ludovisi.

The Mitreo Barberini is here. We found no citable source for how or whether it can be visited - the mapping data's access note is not a source and the official record it points to has gone - so no visiting information for it is given.

The galleries publish their own opening and ticketing information at barberinicorsini.org.

places.name: Piazza Barberini
places.summary: A large square on the rione's boundary, lying across three rioni: Trevi, Colonna and Ludovisi. The Italian Wikipedia article on rione Colonna names Piazza Barberini as Colonna's boundary with Trevi, and no rione holds all of it.
places.history: The Fontana del Tritone stands in the middle of the square, on the Trevi side of the lines that cross it. Roma Capitale's page for that fountain states no rione for it, unlike its pages for the Fontana di Trevi and the Fontana di Monte Cavallo, which both say Trevi.

places.name: Le Quattro Fontane
places.address: Via delle Quattro Fontane, Roma RM
places.summary: Four fountains set into the four corners of a crossroads. Roma Capitale treats them as a single work, the Complesso delle Quattro Fontane, and states no rione for it; the crossroads is shared, three corners falling in Monti and one in Trevi.
places.history: Three of the four corner fountains test in Monti. The fourth, the fountain identified by Roma Capitale as Diana, stands at the corner of the Barberini garden, which tests in Trevi; Roma Capitale records that it was absorbed in 1936 into the Istituto Romano dei Beni Stabili building by Vittorio Morpurgo. That 1936 building is the last radical change Roma Capitale records to the crossroads.

places.name: Resti delle Mura Serviane, Largo Magnanapoli
places.summary: A surviving stretch of the Servian Wall standing in the open at Largo Magnanapoli, in Trevi.
places.history: One warning for anyone working from mapping data: an object of the same name is recorded inside rione Colonna, and that record is an error. The Servian Wall does not run through Colonna.

places.name: Palazzo Valentini and the Domus Romane
places.summary: A palace at Foro Traiano 85, in Trevi, with the Domus Romane beneath it.
places.history: Visits run on arrangements the site publishes itself at palazzovalentini.it. No hours are given here: the ones in circulation come from crowd-sourced mapping data rather than from the institution, so check the site before going.

entries.name: Fontana di Trevi
entries.note: Built 1732-1762 by Nicola Salvi and Giuseppe Pannini against the façade of Palazzo Poli; €2.00 to stand inside the perimeter from 09:00 to 22:00, and free to everyone after the 22:00 closure.

entries.name: Acquedotto Vergine (Aqua Virgo)
entries.note: Inaugurated 19 BC by Agrippa and running over 20 kilometres from Salone, predominantly underground; three travertine arches survive at via del Nazareno, under the inscription recording Claudius's rebuilding in AD 46.

entries.name: Vicus Caprarius - La Città dell'Acqua
entries.note: Excavation at the end of the 1990s uncovered a Neronian insula, a 4th-century domus and a cistern that collected the Acqua Vergine, under the side of the square facing the fountain.

entries.name: Chiesa dei Santi Vincenzo e Anastasio a Trevi
entries.note: The 18 columns on its façade earned it the name il canneto; inside, urns hold the precordia of 22 popes, from Sixtus V to Leo XIII, and they are not displayed.

entries.name: Palazzo del Quirinale
entries.note: Papal residence from 1605 to 1870, royal residence from 1871 to 1946, and the President of the Republic's since; sources disagree on who built it and in which years.

entries.name: Piazza del Quirinale
entries.note: Known as Piazza di Monte Cavallo from the Middle Ages into the 19th century, and laid out from 1586 by Domenico Fontana for Sixtus V; Monti holds part of it and Trevi the rest.

entries.name: Fontana dei Dioscuri (Fontana di Monte Cavallo)
entries.note: A fountain fed by the Acqua Felice stood at the foot of the statues from 1589 until 1783; the present one dates from 1818 and reuses a grey granite basin that had been in the Roman Forum.

entries.name: Obelisco del Quirinale
entries.note: Red Aswan granite, 14.63 m high and 28.94 m with its base and carrying no hieroglyphic inscriptions; Pius VI had it brought from the Mausoleum of Augustus in 1786.

entries.name: Scuderie del Quirinale
entries.note: An 18th-century building by Alessandro Specchi and Ferdinando Fuga, restored between 1997 and 1999 and now used for art exhibitions that change; the venue publishes what is on at scuderiequirinale.it.

entries.name: Accademia Nazionale di San Luca, Palazzo Carpegna
entries.note: Palazzo Carpegna was enlarged and remodelled by Francesco Borromini for Count Ambrogio di Carpegna after 1630 and completed under Francesco Ferrari between 1732 and 1736; the academy and its gallery have been here since 1934.

entries.name: Galleria Sciarra
entries.note: A covered passage built 1886-1888 to Giulio De Angelis's design for Prince Maffeo Sciarra; it is a private courtyard in office use, open to the public during office hours.

entries.name: Palazzo Colonna and the Galleria Colonna
entries.note: The Colonna family's palace on Via della Pilotta, with a picture gallery inside it that opens on a limited schedule published at galleriacolonna.it.

entries.name: Palazzo Barberini and the Gallerie Nazionali d'Arte Antica
entries.note: The palace and its garden on Via delle Quattro Fontane house the Gallerie Nazionali d'Arte Antica, which publish opening and ticketing at barberinicorsini.org; the Mitreo Barberini is here too.

links.note: Colonna's own article names piazza Barberini, via del Tritone, largo Chigi, piazza Colonna and via del Corso as its boundary with Trevi.
Pigna, across via del Corso, holds the Pantheon, Santa Maria sopra Minerva and Palazzo Venezia.
Parione, another of Rome's 22 rioni, holds Piazza Navona and the Palazzo della Cancelleria.
A three-day itinerary across the historic centre, if you are fitting Trevi into a first visit to Rome.
